title: Your own pasture
hookLine: be islands to yourselves; keep to your own ancestral pasture
carry: come back to your own ground

cards: A quail is pecking in open country, far from home, when a hawk drops out of the sky and grabs it.
As it's carried off, the quail laments: if only I'd stayed on my own ground, the ground of my fathers, you'd never have caught me. And where's that? asks the hawk. A plowed field, full of clods.
The hawk, sure of its own strength, lets it go: back you go, then; you won't escape me even there. The quail flies to a big clod, stands on top, and calls out a dare. The hawk dives.
At the last moment the quail slips into a crack in the clod, and the hawk slams breast-first into the earth.

teach.b: That quail story comes from the Connected Discourses, and it brings to life the image that opens the twenty-sixth Long Discourse, the Cakkavatti Sihanada, the lion's roar on the wheel-turning king.
The Buddha is at Matula in Magadha, and he begins: monks, live as islands to yourselves, as your own refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as your island, the Dhamma as your refuge.
Then the image itself: keep to your own pasture, the range of your fathers. Walking there, Mara, the tempter, will get no chance at you.
The Pali for pasture is gocara: range, the ground an animal knows and feeds on. And what is a monk's own pasture?
The Buddha says it plainly: the four foundations of mindfulness. Body, feeling, mind, and mental qualities. That's home ground.
This doesn't mean stay in your bubble, or never go out. The quail isn't safe because it hides. It's safe because it's somewhere it knows well, where it has cover.
The open country, the Connected Discourses say, is the pull of the five senses. Out there, scrolling and comparing and chasing, the hawk can dive.

Back on familiar ground, with attention resting on the breath, the body, what's actually happening, the hawk can't get a grip. The discourse goes on into a long story about kings and the human future.
But it starts with a bird finding its way home.

how: Buddhist meditation teachers often describe the four foundations of mindfulness as the practitioner's home ground, and the hawk-and-quail story is a familiar teaching picture in many Theravada communities.

o: pasture, range: the ground you know
a hiding place far from all danger
the wide-open country of the senses

games.q: your own pasture: tap the pairs.
p: safe among the clods of its own field
struck the ground when it dived

s: 'keep to your own pasture' means never leave your comfort zone
the pasture is the four foundations of mindfulness: attention on familiar ground.
DN 26 opens at Matula, in Magadha
with the call to be islands to yourselves.
the hawk and quail story is told in DN 26 itself
it comes from the Connected Discourses, and makes the same point.

games.q: you're the quail. the hawk has let you go back to your own field, and dared you. what do you do?
o: fly away as far as you can.
stand on a clod in your own field and call out.
stay in the open to prove you're brave.
games.why: the quail calls from a clod in its own field, slips into a crack as the hawk dives, and the hawk hits the clod.

practice: Come back to your own ground: feel the body sitting, one clod in the field; feel the breath, another; notice whether this moment is pleasant or not, another.
When the mind wanders out into the open, into plans or worries or other people's lives, notice the hawk's shadow and step back behind the clod.

wordCard.voice: Gocara. In DN 26 the Buddha says: keep to your own ground, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the tempter gets no chance. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali gocara: pasture, range, the ground an animal knows. in DN 26 it means the four foundations of mindfulness.

carryVoice: Your line: come back to your own ground. Home ground is where the hawk can't get a grip. Day five hundred fifty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 26 (Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta), opening at Matula
Samyutta Nikaya 47.6 (Sakunagghi Sutta), the hawk and the quail
